title: Interface: OCC – Stations – Trains – Field Staff

questions.q: In the interface map Operations Control Centre (OCC) – Stations – Trains – Field staff, the OCC's role is to:
options: Command and coordinate the whole operation
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) is the coordinating brain; the others execute within their areas.

questions.q: In the interface map, stations are responsible for:
options: Issuing movement authorities for the whole line
Managing passengers and the local response at their station
questions.explain: Stations own their passengers and their local ground response.

questions.q: In the interface map, trains (operators) are responsible for:
questions.explain: Trains report what is happening on board and carry out Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s instructions.

questions.q: Field/maintenance staff in the interface map are responsible for:
options: Acting on the ground — attending, repairing and reporting ground truth
questions.explain: Field staff are Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s hands and eyes on the ground.

questions.q: Every operational interface works on two things. They are:
options: A loud voice and good luck
A defined communication channel and a defined authority
A mobile phone and a notebook
questions.explain: Who talks through which channel, and who has final authority — define both and the interface works.

questions.q: Most operational failures are said to be:
questions.explain: Machines usually work; it is the handovers between people/systems that fail — hence interface discipline.

questions.q: An 'interface' in simple words is:
options: The point where two people's jobs touch — who informs whom, through which channel, and who has final authority
questions.explain: Interface = the touching point of two jobs, with information flow and authority defined.

questions.q: A train develops a fault mid-section. The correct interface flow is:
options: Driver repairs it silently without telling anyone
Train reports status to Operations Control Centre (OCC) → OCC coordinates → station/field staff respond as directed
Station staff stop all trains on their own authority
questions.explain: Report up, coordinate at Operations Control Centre (OCC), act where directed — that is the interface chain working.

questions.q: A station sees dangerous overcrowding building on a platform. Its interface duty is to:
options: Close the line on its own
Ask trains to skip without informing Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Inform OCC promptly and manage the crowd locally while OCC regulates trains/information
questions.explain: Stations manage locally AND inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) — both halves of the interface duty.

questions.q: Field staff attending a trackside fault must work under:
options: Coordination with Operations Control Centre (OCC), including power isolation and protection arrangements as required
questions.explain: Ground work touches live railway and power — it happens only inside Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s coordinated plan.

questions.q: Why must a train operator never act on an instruction from an undefined source?
options: Authority is defined — instructions count only when they come through the proper channel from the proper authority
questions.explain: Defined authority prevents conflicting orders — a core interface rule.

questions.q: Operations Control Centre (OCC) asks a station to hold passengers at the concourse during an incident ahead. The station should:
options: Comply, manage passengers locally with announcements, and keep OCC updated
Send passengers to the platform anyway
Close the station without informing OCC
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) coordinates, stations execute locally and report back — a two-way interface.

questions.q: A field team finishes a repair. To restore normal working, they must:
options: Just walk away — trains will find out
Report completion/clearance to Operations Control Centre (OCC), which coordinates restoration of services and power
questions.explain: Restoration is coordinated from Operations Control Centre (OCC) after the ground reports clear — nobody self-restores.

questions.q: Confusion between a station and a train about who should make an announcement during a fault is an example of:
options: An interface failure — roles at the touching point were not clear
questions.explain: The equipment worked; the hand-over of responsibility did not — a textbook interface failure.

questions.q: Which channel is the defined link between a train operator and Operations Control Centre (OCC)?
questions.explain: The recorded radio with the train's identity is the defined Operations Control Centre (OCC)–train channel.

questions.q: During a power isolation for track work, the interfaces involved are mainly:
options: Power Controller/Operations Control Centre (OCC) ↔ field staff ↔ train controller, keeping trains clear while the section is made safe
questions.explain: Isolation touches power, trains and ground staff together — Operations Control Centre (OCC) holds the coordination.

questions.q: A station receives two conflicting instructions from two different people. Correct action?
options: Follow the defined authority (Operations Control Centre (OCC)) and seek clarification through the proper channel
questions.explain: Defined authority exists exactly for this moment — escalate to Operations Control Centre (OCC) and clarify.

questions.q: Ground truth — what is actually happening at a site — reaches Operations Control Centre (OCC) mainly through:
options: Reports from trains, stations and field staff
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) decides on what its interfaces report; accurate ground reporting is therefore a safety duty.

questions.q: Why does the extract say interface failures dominate over equipment failures in exams?
options: Because interfaces are not in the syllabus
Because exam scenarios usually test who informs whom, through which channel, and who decides — not whether a machine works
Because Operations Control Centre (OCC) does everything itself
questions.explain: Scenario questions are interface questions: information, channel, authority.

questions.q: A train operator notices a lineside defect while passing. His interface action is:
options: Note it for the monthly report only
Report it promptly to Operations Control Centre (OCC) with location details so field staff can be directed
questions.explain: Report position and nature to Operations Control Centre (OCC) — the system then tasks the right people.

questions.q: Platform Screen Door (PSD) fault at a platform: which interfaces act together?
options: Only the Automatic Fare Collection (AFC) supervisor
Station staff (isolate/supervise) ↔ Operations Control Centre (OCC) (informed, regulates) ↔ train operator (berthing/door coordination)
questions.explain: A Platform Screen Door (PSD) fault touches station, Operations Control Centre (OCC) and train together — a live example of the interface map.

questions.q: If a station's local response and Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s network plan conflict during an emergency, what resolves it?
options: The defined authority — OCC coordinates the network response while the station manages its local area within that plan
questions.explain: Local management inside a centrally coordinated plan — that division is the interface design.

questions.q: A maintenance team needs a section of track. The request flows:
options: Field/maintenance need → coordinated by Operations Control Centre (OCC) (with power controller/train controller) → protection and isolation arranged → work permitted
questions.explain: Possession-type work is granted through coordination, never self-taken.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a healthy interface?
options: A station hears of an incident from passengers first
A driver reports a fault on the recorded radio; Operations Control Centre (OCC) acknowledges, tasks the station and field staff, and updates the driver
Field staff learn of a plan from a notice board
questions.explain: Report – acknowledge – task – update: the loop closing is the sign of a working interface.

questions.q: Information about a disruption reaches passengers best when interfaces work in this order:
options: Each station invents its own version
Trains/stations report to OCC → OCC approves one version → stations/trains announce it through Passenger Information System (PIS)/Public Address System (PAS)
questions.explain: One verified version flowing outward is why the Operations Control Centre (OCC) sits at the centre of the map.

questions.q: A new operator is unsure whether a task is his, the station's, or Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s. The syllabus answer is to check:
options: The defined interface — whose job touches that point, through which channel, and who holds authority
questions.explain: Interfaces are defined in advance precisely so nobody has to guess during an incident.

questions.q: Why are field staff reports called 'ground truth'?
options: Because they work on the ground floor
Because Operations Control Centre (OCC) has no information
Because they describe what is physically true at the site, against which OCC's plan is checked
Because reports are written on paper
questions.explain: Screens show indications; field staff confirm reality — Operations Control Centre (OCC) plans on their truth.

questions.q: During simultaneous problems at two stations, Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s interface role is to:
options: Prioritise and coordinate both responses, tasking stations/trains/field staff in order
Stop the entire network in all cases
questions.explain: Coordination and prioritisation across the whole line is exactly what Operations Control Centre (OCC) exists for.

questions.q: Which pairing of role and responsibility is WRONG?
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC) — driving each train personally
Field staff — act on the ground
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) coordinates; it does not drive trains — operators do.

questions.q: The whole Unit ii interface lesson in one line is:
options: Equipment rarely fails the railway; undefined channels and unclear authority do — so every interface fixes its channel and its authority in advance
Only Operations Control Centre (OCC) needs to communicate
questions.explain: Channel + authority, defined before the incident — that is the examinable core of interfaces.

questions.q: Shift handover between outgoing and incoming controllers and station staff is itself an important interface because:
options: It is a formality with no operational content
Ongoing incidents, isolations, defects and special instructions must pass completely and clearly to the next shift — a poor handover loses the ground truth the previous shift held
Only attendance is marked at handover
questions.explain: The railway runs 24×7 but people work in shifts. A disciplined, logged handover is how the Operations Control Centre (OCC) picture survives a change of people.

questions.q: The depot is another interface in daily operations. Bringing trains into service for the first service of the day requires coordination between:
options: The depot (train preparation and despatch), the Operations Control Centre (OCC) (accepting and regulating the train) and the first station (passenger readiness)
questions.explain: A train does not simply 'appear' for the first service. Depot despatch, Operations Control Centre (OCC) acceptance and station readiness must meet at the same minute — an interface repeated at every induction and withdrawal.

questions.q: Certain safety-critical authorities — for example, authorising a train to pass a signal at danger — are given as written or formally recorded orders, not casual verbal messages, because:
options: A written/recorded authority is exact, can be read back and checked, and remains as proof of what was authorised, by whom and when
Verbal orders are banned for all purposes
questions.explain: The more safety-critical the instruction, the more formal its interface. Written or recorded authority removes memory and misunderstanding from the most dangerous permissions in operations.

questions.q: Where the Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) meets another railway or an adjacent control area, operations must also manage an external interface. Its main need is:
options: Coordinated decisions at the boundary — train movements, power and emergencies on one side affect the other, so the two controls must plan and inform each other
Using the same uniform for staff
questions.explain: No control area is an island. At a boundary, the Operations Control Centre (OCC) and the neighbouring control work as one interface, especially during through running and emergencies.

questions.q: During a major incident at a site, one named incident coordinator is appointed on the ground mainly to:
options: Be the single point of contact between the site and the Operations Control Centre (OCC), so instructions flow through one channel and parallel, conflicting orders are avoided
Replace the Operations Control Centre (OCC) completely
Count the passengers at the site
questions.explain: Many agencies work at an incident site, but the interface to the Operations Control Centre (OCC) must stay single and clear — one coordinator speaking for the site prevents crossed instructions.
